claims.text: Pulumi has a defined provider support policy that specifies how long Pulumi maintains each provider major version, and which providers get long-term security updates.
Pulumi publishes a 'Provider support policy' page at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/.
Some Pulumi providers receive long-term security updates while others do not.
Pulumi does not automatically roll back changes made during an update if an error or failure occurs.
When an error or failure occurs during a Pulumi update, Pulumi completes any pending operations currently in progress and then exits and reports the error or failure.

To accomplish a manual rollback after a failed Pulumi deployment, you revert the code and configuration changes of the failed deployment and run `pulumi up` to update your infrastructure to its previous state.
Pulumi does not automatically query your cloud provider's live state before running `pulumi up` or `pulumi preview`.
Pulumi's `pulumi up` and `pulumi preview` commands compare the desired state declared in your program against the last recorded state to determine what changes to make.
Refreshing state requires a round-trip to the cloud provider for every resource in a stack, which adds significant latency, especially for large stacks.
Running `pulumi refresh` synchronizes Pulumi's recorded state with the actual state of your cloud resources.
`pulumi up --refresh` refreshes and applies your desired state in a single step.
Pulumi Cloud provides built-in drift detection for automated drift detection and remediation on a schedule.

Pulumi resources have different logical names and physical names, where the logical name is part of the auto-assigned resource URN and only needs to be unique within a stack, while the physical name typically needs to be unique within a certain scope, sometimes globally.

Pulumi automatically creates each resource's physical name by combining the logical name with a random suffix appended afterward, to allow many logical Pulumi resources and stacks to be stood up side-by-side without conflicting.
Pulumi's auto-naming approach ensures Pulumi can replace resources with less downtime by creating the replacement before needing to delete the old resource.
With Pulumi's default auto-naming, a resource's physical name will typically look like `my-bucket-d7c2fa0` instead of `my-bucket`.

Pulumi lets you disable auto-naming on a per-resource basis to have precise physical names without random suffixes, at the cost of losing the two named benefits (safe side-by-side stand-up and lower-downtime replacement).
Pulumi lets you use project or stack configuration to customize or disable auto-naming globally, per provider, or per resource type.
Pulumi provides primitives so that secrets can be stored in a secure manner in the CLI, state file, and Pulumi Cloud.
During a Pulumi update, secrets are decrypted in memory and visible to the Pulumi program.
Passing `--secret` to `pulumi config set` causes the configuration value to be encrypted so it can be safely persisted in `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml`.
For every stack, Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key that it uses to encrypt secrets for that stack, and this is configurable to use a custom secrets provider instead.

Because a different encryption key is used for each stack, encrypting the same value across two different stacks produces different encrypted strings in the respective `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` files.
You cannot copy an encrypted secret value from one `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` file to another using a text editor; you must instead use `pulumi config set`.

When you run a Pulumi preview, update, or destroy, Pulumi decrypts secret configuration data, and it is plain text during the execution of the deployment, accessible to any part of the Pulumi program via the Pulumi config object.
Pulumi does not use the Terraform engine in any way.
Some Pulumi providers use the open-source Terraform schemas in order to know what resources and parameters are available, and to determine the return and response attributes.
Pulumi native providers are mapped directly to the cloud provider APIs and do not use Terraform schemas.
Pulumi is a declarative tool that uses imperative languages to define your end state, where the language is used for authoring the program but not for talking to the cloud provider API.
Pulumi uses strongly typed languages with programming languages that support IntelliSense and the Language Server Protocol, meaning you rarely need to leave your IDE when defining Pulumi programs.
Experimental Pulumi features are always opt-in, requiring explicit enabling via a flag, command, or environment variable such as `PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true`.
Experimental Pulumi features are not necessarily supported and can change or be removed at any time without a deprecation cycle.
`PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true` is an environment variable used to enable experimental Pulumi functionality.
Pulumi focuses on actively supporting the latest released major version of the providers it maintains.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version for up to a year, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The Pulumi provider support policy page lists the covered providers and what a long-term support release contains.
Older major versions of Pulumi providers receive no patches at all.
You can find the current version for all providers maintained by Pulumi in the Pulumi Registry.

When a major version of a Pulumi provider is released, that is a signal to begin planning a provider version update, since major versions typically include significant changes such as deprecations, new resources, and new functionality that may require additional migration steps.
Pulumi recommends that, at least quarterly, you consider updating to the latest minor version on the current major and minimally review provider release notes.
Minor versions of Pulumi providers typically include new resources and features, as well as performance improvements and bug fixes, without introducing breaking changes.
The release notes for each Pulumi provider release summarize the new capabilities or fixes so users can identify changes relevant to their usage.
Pulumi recommends always allowing patch updates on the current minor version, for example using the tilde operator in npm (e.g. ~1.2.3).
Patch versions of Pulumi providers are primarily for bug fixes and security updates and are designed to be fully backward compatible.
Pulumi recommends never being 2 major versions behind on a provider, since it is inadvisable to jump a major version due to the number of potential breaking changes across major versions.

Each major version of a Pulumi provider includes migration logic to smooth the upgrade from the immediately previous major version, but these migrations do not always work across multiple major versions.
The 'Provider support policy' link points to /docs/support/provider-support-policy/, a page describing Pulumi's provider version support policy.
Pulumi actively maintains the latest released major version of every provider it publishes.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version for up to 12 months, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
There is a current list of providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
The AWS provider (/registry/packages/aws/) receives Pulumi long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
The Azure Classic provider (/registry/packages/azure/) receives Pulumi long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
The Azure Native provider (/registry/packages/azure-native/) receives Pulumi long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
The Azure AD provider (/registry/packages/azuread/) receives Pulumi long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
The Command provider (/registry/packages/command/) receives Pulumi long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
The Docker Build provider (/registry/packages/docker-build/) receives Pulumi long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
The GCP provider (/registry/packages/gcp/) receives Pulumi long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
The Kubernetes provider (/registry/packages/kubernetes/) receives Pulumi long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
The TLS provider (/registry/packages/tls/) receives Pulumi long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
The Vault provider (/registry/packages/vault/) receives Pulumi long-term support updates on eligible older versions.
An LTS provider release ships fixes for CVEs affecting the provider's code or its direct dependencies, and fixes for broken internal infrastructure on the LTS branch needed to ship those CVE fixes.

An LTS provider release does not contain new upstream API versions, new resources or new resource properties, performance improvements, non-security bug fixes, or compatibility updates for newer language runtime versions.
Providers remain compatible with the version of Pulumi they were frozen at unless otherwise prompted via security fixes.
Exactly one long-term support major version exists per provider at any time.

When a provider's major version N+1 ships, N+1 becomes the new current major, N becomes the new LTS major, and the previous LTS major reaches end of life on the same day regardless of how much of its 12-month window remained.
Within a provider's long-term support major version, only the latest minor version receives patches, and earlier minors are frozen.
LTS provider releases are available through the same standard package registries as current-major releases, but are tagged differently.
Customers pinning to a specific provider major version will automatically receive patch releases as they ship.
Pinning to a specific major version is the recommended approach for consuming provider releases.
At any time, exactly one major version of a covered provider is the LTS version, and older major versions receive no patches.
If v3 is the newest release of a covered provider, then v3 is N, v2 is N-1 (the LTS version), and v1 and earlier versions are end of life.
The current major version (N) of a covered provider receives new features, new resources, bug fixes, security patches, dependency upgrades, and new upstream API versions until N+1 ships.

The long-term support version (N-1) of a covered provider receives security updates in the provider's code or its direct dependencies for up to 12 months from N's release, or until N+1 ships, whichever comes first.
Provider versions at N-2 and older are end of life, are not supported, and will not receive updates.
There is a page titled "Best practices for maintaining provider versions" at /docs/support/faq/infrastructure/#what-are-the-best-practices-for-maintaining-provider-versions.
There is a Pulumi Registry page at /registry/.
There is a "Getting support" page at /docs/support/getting-support/.
